items.stem: What is the area of a triangle with base 10 cm and height 7 cm?
items.answer: 35 cm²

items.stem: Explain why all triangles with base 5 cm whose top vertex lies on a line parallel to the base, 7 cm above it, have the same area.
items.answer: They all have the same base 5 cm and the same perpendicular height 7 cm, so each area is ½ × 5 × 7 = 17.5 cm².
items.markingKey: Same base and perpendicular height (R1); area value (A1).

items.stem: Explain where the formula ½(a + b)h for a trapezium comes from.
items.answer: Two identical trapeziums, one rotated, form a parallelogram with base a + b and height h; one trapezium is half of it.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Two identical trapeziums, one rotated, form a parallelogram with base a + b and height h; one trapezium is half of it. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "The area of a triangle with base 8 and height 6 is 48." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Area = ½ × base × height = 24; 48 is the rectangle.
items.markingKey: Area = ½ × base × height = 24; 48 is the rectangle. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A trapezium has area 202 cm² and parallel sides 13 cm and 18 cm. Find its height.

items.answer: (a) 1 × 11 up to 6 × 6 (b) areas from 11 to 36 cm² (c) the closer to a square, the larger the area; largest 6 × 6
items.markingKey: (a) 1 × 11 up to 6 × 6 (b) areas from 11 to 36 cm² (c) the closer to a square, the larger the area; largest 6 × 6. Correct area formula (M1 A1); rounding up / pattern recognised (B or D: M1 A1); justified conclusion (R1).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why π is the same for every circle.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "curved surface area of a cylinder".
items.answer: The area of the rectangle that wraps around it: 2πrh
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the area of the rectangle that wraps around it: 2πrh. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "cross-section"?
options: The volume of a cube with edge 1 cm; 1 cm³ = 1000 mm³ = 1 mL
The area of the rectangle that wraps around it: 2πrh
The 2D shape you see when a solid is sliced; for a prism it is the same all the way along
The amount of flat surface a 2D shape covers, measured in square units
items.answer: The 2D shape you see when a solid is sliced; for a prism it is the same all the way along
items.markingKey: C. "cross-section" is the 2D shape you see when a solid is sliced; for a prism it is the same all the way along.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "compound shape"?
options: The amount of space a 3D shape occupies, measured in cubic units
The total area of all the faces (surfaces) of a 3D shape
A shape made by joining or removing simpler shapes such as rectangles and triangles
A quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides; area = ½(a + b)h
items.answer: A shape made by joining or removing simpler shapes such as rectangles and triangles
items.markingKey: C. "compound shape" is a shape made by joining or removing simpler shapes such as rectangles and triangles.

items.stem: A student claims: "The circumference of a circle of radius 5 is π × 5 = 15.7." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: C = 2πr = 10π ≈ 31.4; πr uses the radius instead of the diameter.
items.markingKey: C = 2πr = 10π ≈ 31.4; πr uses the radius instead of the diameter. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Elena says 3 m² = 300 cm² because there are 100 cm in a metre. Explain the error, using a diagram of a 1 m square, and give the correct value.
items.answer: A 1 m square is 100 cm × 100 cm = 10 000 cm², so 3 m² = 30 000 cm²; both dimensions must be converted.
items.markingKey: Square diagram reasoning (R1); correct factor 10 000 (A1); value (A1).

items.stem: Ingrid doubles every edge of a cube of side 8 cm. Explain how the surface area changes.
items.answer: 384 cm² → 1536 cm²: four times as big, because each face area is multiplied by 2² = 4.
items.markingKey: Both surface areas (A1); scale factor squared (R1).

items.stem: Explain why doubling the radius of a cylinder multiplies its volume by 4 but doubling its height only doubles it.
items.answer: V = πr²h: r is squared, so ×2 gives ×4, while h appears once.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: V = πr²h: r is squared, so ×2 gives ×4, while h appears once. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Hana writes: "The area of a triangle with base 8 and height 6 is 48." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Area = ½ × base × height = 24; 48 is the rectangle.
items.markingKey: Area = ½ × base × height = 24; 48 is the rectangle. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Felix says that if the radius of a circular pizza is multiplied by 3, there is 3 times as much pizza. Explain whether this is correct, using r = 8 cm.
items.answer: Not correct: area 64π → 576π cm², 9 times as much, because area depends on r².
items.markingKey: Both areas (A1); factor k² explained (R1).

items.stem: "3 cm³ = 30 mm³." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: 1 cm³ = 1000 mm³, so 3 cm³ = 3000 mm³.
items.markingKey: 1 cm³ = 1000 mm³, so 3 cm³ = 3000 mm³. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "The surface area of a closed cylinder is 2πrh." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: That is only the curved surface; add the two circular ends 2πr².
items.markingKey: That is only the curved surface; add the two circular ends 2πr². 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "1 litre = 100 cm³." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: 1 litre = 1000 cm³ (a 10 cm cube).
items.markingKey: 1 litre = 1000 cm³ (a 10 cm cube). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A trapezium has area 116 cm² and parallel sides 5 cm and 16 cm. Find its height.
items.answer: 11 cm

items.stem: A circular pond has an area of 1520.5 m². Find its diameter, to the nearest metre.
How many 250 mL glasses can be filled from a 3.1 litre jug?
items.answer: 12 glasses

items.stem: Find the total surface area of a cuboid measuring 12 cm by 7 cm by 3 cm.
items.answer: 282 cm²

items.stem: Sugar cubes of side 1 cm are packed into a box 6 cm × 6 cm × 8 cm. (a) How many cubes fit? (b) The sugar is then poured into a cylindrical jar of radius 6 cm and height 18 cm. Will it fit? (c) Explain why the sugar takes up less space when poured.
items.answer: (a) 288 (b) jar volume 2040 cm³ ≥ 288 cm³: yes (c) loose sugar can fill gaps, but the total volume of the sugar itself stays the same
items.markingKey: (a) 288 (b) jar volume 2040 cm³ ≥ 288 cm³: yes (c) loose sugar can fill gaps, but the total volume of the sugar itself stays the same. Volume calculated (M1 A1); unit conversion (A1); rate/comparison (M1 A1); interpretation (D: R1).

items.stem: A school garden in Dubai is a trapezium with parallel sides 10 m and 8 m, 10 m apart. (a) Find its area. (b) Grass seed is sold in boxes covering 2.5 m² for AED 1.89. How many boxes are needed and what is the cost? (c) Suggest why the gardener might buy one extra box.
items.answer: (a) 90 m² (b) 36 boxes, AED 68.04 (c) to allow for wastage or uneven sowing
items.markingKey: (a) 90 m² (b) 36 boxes, AED 68.04 (c) to allow for wastage or uneven sowing. Correct area formula (M1 A1); rounding up / pattern recognised (B or D: M1 A1); justified conclusion (R1).

items.stem: A bicycle wheel in Vienna has a diameter of 0.63 m. (a) Find its circumference to 3 s.f. (b) How many complete turns does it make on a 8 km ride? (c) Explain one reason why the real number of turns may differ.
items.answer: (a) 1.98 m (b) 4042 complete turns (c) tyre pressure/wear changes the effective diameter; the path is not perfectly straight
items.markingKey: (a) 1.98 m (b) 4042 complete turns (c) tyre pressure/wear changes the effective diameter; the path is not perfectly straight. Correct circle formulae (M1 A1); multi-step calculation (M1 A1); interpretation / limitation in context (D: R1).

items.stem: A roof in Toronto has a horizontal area of 109 m². During a storm 15 mm of rain falls. (a) Convert 15 mm to metres. (b) Find the volume of water that falls on the roof in m³. (c) How many litres is that? (d) How many 200-litre barrels would it fill?
items.answer: (a) 0.015 m (b) 1.635 m³ (c) 1635 L (d) 8 full barrels
items.markingKey: (a) 0.015 m (b) 1.635 m³ (c) 1635 L (d) 8 full barrels. Consistent units (M1 A1); area/volume calculation (M1 A1); practical rounding and explanation (D: R1).
